dedupe_keys.name: payment system design and participant operational disruptions in australia s rtgs system rba rdp 2012 05

description: This study simulates what happens in Australia's real-time gross settlement system, RITS, when one participant bank suffers an operational disruption and becomes a liquidity sink, holding funds that other banks need to settle their payments. It compares five system designs, from pure real-time gross settlement to designs with a central queue, a bilateral-offset algorithm and sub-limits, and varies how fast other banks react. It was written by Ashwin Clarke and Jennifer Hancock and published by the Reserve Bank of Australia as Research Discussion Paper 2012-05 in September 2012. It uses the Bank of Finland's BoF-PSS2 simulator with RITS transaction, liquidity and sub-limit data for 10 business days in early 2008, when about 191 billion Australian dollars settled daily using some 15 billion of liquidity. The paper is free online in HTML and PDF, under the Bank's copyright. Findings: hybrid features generally mitigate systemic impact, with the bilateral offset plus sub-limits most effective, though less so if banks hold less liquidity. Caveats: results come from one fortnight of 2008 and the paper states its results are preliminary. For simulation it is a worked example of cascading liquidity failure in a payment network, reusable when modelling outages of banks that serve energy, water or transport operators. It is related to the BoF-PSS2 simulator record in this catalogue, the tool it used.

name: Payment system design and participant operational disruptions in Australia's RTGS system (RBA RDP 2012-05)
outcomes: Hybrid features reduce the systemic impact of a participant's operational disruption; a bilateral-offset algorithm combined with sub-limits is most effective, but its benefit shrinks if banks hold less liquidity, and sub-limits help only if participants stop paying the stricken bank; no firm conclusion on a central queue alone
